questions.prompt: A dataset has 2% positives. A model that predicts negative for every case has which property?
questions.explanation: Always-negative gets every negative right (98%) and misses every positive (recall 0). Accuracy alone hides this.

questions.prompt: TP=45, FP=15, FN=5, TN=935. What is the precision? (decimal, 3 places, tolerance 0.001)
A detector has TP=45, FP=15, FN=5, TN=935. What is the F1 score? (decimal, tolerance 0.001)
A calibrated classifier. A false negative costs 4 and a false positive costs 1. At what probability should you start predicting positive? (decimal, tolerance 0.001)
questions.explanation: Predict positive when p·4>(1−p)·1, i.e. p>1/5=0.2.

questions.prompt: You evaluate 30 configurations on the validation set, choose the best and report its validation score as the expected performance. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing is wrong: validation data is by definition unbiased for the chosen model.
The learning rate should have been larger, so the search must be repeated.
The best of many noisy scores is optimistically biased; report on untouched test data.
The score is pessimistic, because the chosen model saw less training data than the others.
questions.explanation: Selection on the validation set uses it up; the maximum of many noisy estimates overstates true performance.

questions.prompt: Probabilities from a model have an ECE of 0.18 on the test set. What does this say?
options: On average, stated confidence differs from observed frequency by about 0.18 across bins.
The model overfits: the training loss is 0.18 lower than the loss on the test set.
The ranking of the examples is wrong, since ECE measures how well scores order the cases.
The accuracy is 82%, since ECE equals one minus the accuracy of the model on the test set.
questions.explanation: ECE is a weighted average gap between confidence and observed frequency; it says nothing directly about accuracy or ranking.

questions.prompt: Your detector reports precision 0.9 on a balanced test set. It will run where positives are 1% of the cases. What do you check and report before deployment?
rubric: Explains that precision depends on prevalence and recomputes it (Bayes) or re-evaluates on data with deployment prevalence.
Reports recall/false-alarm rate and the cost of each error, and a trivial baseline.
Checks calibration or recalibrates scores for the new prior, and names a way the result could be rejected.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
